section.title: Daniel's Prayer and the Seventy Weeks
section.sectionRationale: Reading in Jeremiah that the exile would last seventy years, Daniel pours out one of Scripture's great prayers of confession, pleading God's mercy for His people and city. God answers through Gabriel with the prophecy of the seventy weeks, a sweeping timetable of what God will accomplish for sin and for His holy city, culminating in an Anointed One who makes atonement and is cut off. It joins heartfelt repentance to the deepest promise of redemption in the book.
section.thesis: Daniel confesses his people's sin and appeals only to God's mercy and covenant faithfulness, and God answers not merely with release from Babylon but with the promise of seventy weeks in which an Anointed Prince will finish transgression, atone for iniquity, and bring in everlasting righteousness, though He is cut off to do it.
section.frameNote: Five beats: Daniel reads Jeremiah and turns to prayer; the confession of sin; the plea for mercy for God's own sake; Gabriel comes swiftly with an answer; and the prophecy of the seventy weeks and the Anointed One who is cut off.

verses.text: In the first year of Darius son of Xerxes, a Mede by descent, who was made ruler over the kingdom of the Chaldeans,
in the first year of his reign, I, Daniel, understood from the sacred books, according to the word of the LORD to Jeremiah the prophet, that the desolation of Jerusalem would last seventy years.
So I turned my attention to the Lord God to seek Him by prayer and petition, with fasting, sackcloth, and ashes.
And I prayed to the LORD my God and confessed, “O, Lord, the great and awesome God, who keeps His covenant of {{chesed|loving devotion}} to those who love Him and keep His commandments,
we have sinned and done wrong. We have acted wickedly and rebelled. We have turned away from Your commandments and ordinances.
We have not listened to Your servants the prophets, who spoke in Your name to our kings, leaders, fathers, and all the people of the land.

To You, O Lord, belongs righteousness, but this day we are covered with shame, the men of Judah, the people of Jerusalem, and all Israel near and far, in all the countries to which You have driven us because of our unfaithfulness to You.
O LORD, we are covered with shame, our kings, our leaders, and our fathers, because we have sinned against You.
To the Lord our God belong compassion and forgiveness, even though we have rebelled against Him
and have not obeyed the voice of the LORD our God to walk in His laws, which He set before us through His servants the prophets.

All Israel has transgressed Your law and turned away, refusing to obey Your voice; so the oath and the curse written in the Law of Moses the servant of God has been poured out on us, because we have sinned against You.
You have carried out the words spoken against us and against our rulers by bringing upon us a great disaster. For under all of heaven, nothing has ever been done like what has been done to Jerusalem.
Just as it is written in the Law of Moses, all this disaster has come upon us, yet we have not sought the favor of the LORD our God by turning from our iniquities and giving attention to Your truth.
Therefore the LORD has kept the calamity in store and brought it upon us. For the LORD our God is righteous in all He does; yet we have not obeyed His voice.

units.label: The plea for mercy for God's own sake
units.note: not for our righteousness, but Your compassion

verses.text: Now, O Lord our God, who brought Your people out of the land of Egypt with a mighty hand, and who made for Yourself a name renowned to this day, we have sinned; we have acted wickedly.

O Lord, in keeping with all Your righteous acts, I pray that Your anger and wrath may turn away from Your city Jerusalem, Your holy mountain; for because of our sins and the iniquities of our fathers, Jerusalem and Your people are a reproach to all around us.
So now, our God, hear the prayers and petitions of Your servant. For Your sake, O Lord, cause Your face to shine upon Your desolate sanctuary.

Incline Your ear, O my God, and hear; open Your eyes and see the desolation of the city that bears Your name. For we are not presenting our petitions before You because of our righteous acts, but because of Your great compassion.
O Lord, listen! O Lord, forgive! O Lord, hear and act! For Your sake, O my God, do not delay, because Your city and Your people bear Your name.”
While I was speaking, praying, confessing my sin and that of my people Israel, and presenting my petition before the LORD my God concerning His holy mountain,
while I was still praying, Gabriel, the man I had seen in the earlier vision, came to me in swift flight about the time of the evening sacrifice.
He instructed me and spoke with me, saying: “O Daniel, I have come now to give you insight and understanding.
At the beginning of your petitions, an answer went out, and I have come to tell you, for you are highly precious. So consider the message and understand the vision:

units.label: The prophecy of the seventy weeks
units.note: atonement and the Anointed One cut off

verses.text: {{shavuim|Seventy weeks}} are decreed for your people and your holy city to stop their transgression, to put an end to sin, to make {{kaphar|atonement}} for iniquity, to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal up vision and prophecy, and to anoint the Most Holy Place.

Know and understand this: From the issuance of the decree to restore and rebuild Jerusalem until the {{mashiach|Messiah}}, the Prince, there will be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. It will be rebuilt with streets and a trench, but in times of distress.

Then after the sixty-two weeks the Messiah will be cut off and will have nothing. Then the people of the prince who is to come will destroy the city and the sanctuary. The end will come like a flood, and until the end there will be war; desolations have been decreed.

And he will confirm a covenant with many for one week, but in the middle of the week he will put an end to sacrifice and offering. And on the wing of the temple will come the abomination that causes desolation, until the decreed destruction is poured out upon him.”

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant love, mercy, and loyalty. Daniel appeals to the God who keeps His covenant of chesed, resting his whole prayer not on Israel's worthiness but on God's faithful, unbreakable love. It is the ground of hope for a guilty people: God's own loyal love.

shavuim.gloss: Sevens, or weeks. Seventy shavuim, seventy sevens, are decreed for Daniel's people and city. The word answers Jeremiah's seventy years and stretches them into a longer, symbolic span of God's redemptive plan, reaching its center in the work of the Anointed One.

kaphar.gloss: To make atonement, to cover or wipe away sin, to reconcile. At the heart of the seventy weeks is the promise to make kaphar for iniquity, the deepest goal of the whole prophecy. It points beyond the temple sacrifices to the once-for-all atonement accomplished by the Anointed One who is cut off.

mashiach.gloss: Anointed One, Messiah, the one set apart with oil for God's service, especially as king or priest. The prophecy names the coming of the Messiah, the Prince, who will then be cut off, and Christians read this as pointing directly to Jesus, the Anointed One who dies to atone for sin.

basic.context: Daniel, now an old man, is reading Jeremiah and realizes the seventy years of exile are nearly over. Rather than simply wait, he throws himself into prayer, confessing the sins of his people with deep humility and pleading for mercy, not because they deserve it but because of God's compassion and His own name. As he prays, the angel Gabriel arrives with an answer far greater than release from Babylon: the prophecy of the seventy weeks, God's timetable to deal with sin once and for all and to bring in everlasting righteousness through an Anointed One who is cut off.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter has two halves that belong together: a model prayer of confession and a dense prophecy. Daniel prays Scripture back to God, resting entirely on grace. The seventy weeks are among the most debated verses in the Bible, and faithful Christians differ on the exact scheme. What is clear, and central, is the sixfold goal of verse 24, finishing sin and making atonement, fulfilled in the Messiah who is cut off.
basic.originalLanguages: Daniel appeals to the God of chesed, covenant loving devotion. The answer is seventy shavuim, sevens, in which God will make kaphar, atonement, for iniquity. And the prophecy names the mashiach, the Anointed One, the Messiah who comes and is then cut off.
basic.typology: The daily and yearly sacrifices, and the Day of Atonement's covering of sin, all point to the atonement promised here, which the Messiah accomplishes in His death. The desolate sanctuary Daniel weeps over gives way to the true and final cleansing achieved when the Anointed One is cut off to atone for iniquity.
basic.christ: The seventy weeks reach their goal in the Messiah, the Prince, who is cut off but not for Himself. Jesus is the Anointed One whose death makes atonement for iniquity and brings in everlasting righteousness, exactly the six things verse 24 promises. Daniel's plea for God to forgive for His own sake is answered supremely at the cross.
basic.god: God is righteous in all His judgments, yet rich in compassion and forgiveness, keeping covenant love with an undeserving people. He hears prayer swiftly, answers beyond what is asked, and is working a plan that runs through the centuries to deal with sin forever. He acts for His own name's sake, which is the surest ground of hope.
basic.crossReferences: Jeremiah 25 and 29 give the seventy years Daniel is reading. Leviticus 16 describes the atonement the Messiah fulfills. And Matthew 24 and Hebrews 9 pick up the ending of sacrifice and the once-for-all atonement of Christ.
basic.oneStory: Daniel's confession voices the whole exile's need: a sinful people who can appeal only to grace. God's answer lifts their eyes past release from Babylon to the real deliverance, the Anointed One who finishes transgression and atones for sin. The seventy weeks trace the line from exile straight to the cross, where the deepest desolation is answered by everlasting righteousness.

context.literary:
Daniel 9 is built as a hinge between two kinds of speech. Verses 1 to 19 are a prayer that Daniel speaks up to heaven; verses 20 to 27 are an oracle that Gabriel speaks down to earth. The first half is plain, first person, and full of the vocabulary of Israel's worship. The second is compressed, numerical, and so dense that nearly every phrase has been argued over. The two halves are joined by timing, because the answer arrives while the prayer is still in his mouth, verse 20, and Gabriel says it was issued at the start of the petitions, verse 23.

The prayer has its own clear shape. It opens by naming God as great and awesome and covenant keeping, verse 4. It then confesses in a rising spiral, first the guilt of the people, verses 5 to 6, then the contrast of God's righteousness and our shame, verses 7 to 14, which is stated twice, once at verse 7 and again at verse 14. The turn comes at verse 15 with the word now, and the petition runs to verse 19 with a staccato close: Lord, listen, Lord, forgive, Lord, hear and act. Notice that the confession is long and the request short. Daniel spends fourteen verses on the problem before he asks for anything.

The book itself changes language and genre around this point. Chapters 2 to 7 were Aramaic court tales and a dream vision; chapters 8 to 12 are in Hebrew and are all visions interpreted by an angel. Chapter 9 is the only one of these in which Daniel is not frightened or overwhelmed by what he sees. He is a reader, with a scroll, and the vision grows out of study and prayer. It sits between the ram and goat of chapter 8, which ended with an unexplained "evening and morning" and a sanctuary trampled, and the great final revelation of chapters 10 to 12, which will return to the same desecration in detail. Chapter 9 supplies the reason behind both: sin must be dealt with before the sanctuary can be restored.
context.historical:
The setting is the very first year of the Persian takeover of Babylon, about 539 BC. Daniel is probably in his eighties, a survivor of the first deportation of 605 BC, Daniel 1:1. The "Darius the Mede" of verse 1 is introduced as one set over the realm, not as its founder, and his precise identity is still discussed; the text only says that he was made ruler of the Chaldeans. What matters here is that Daniel does his arithmetic at a moment of political change.

The seventy years come from Jeremiah, who wrote to the first exiles and told them to build houses and seek the welfare of the city where they lived, and who also said that after seventy years God would visit them, Jeremiah 29:10. Jeremiah 25:11 to 12 says Babylon would be punished when the seventy years ended. The Chronicler adds that the land lay desolate to enjoy its Sabbaths, 2 Chronicles 36:21, reading the exile against the Torah's rule that the land must rest, Leviticus 26:34 to 35. Israel had ignored many Sabbath years, and God would collect them.

The prayer is soaked in older texts. The opening address echoes Deuteronomy 7:9 and Nehemiah 1:5. The confession uses the four verbs of Solomon's temple prayer, which anticipated exactly this exile, 1 Kings 8:46 to 50. The reference to the curse "written in the Law of Moses" is a reference to Deuteronomy 28 and 29. Daniel is not making up words but praying Scripture, and doing it on behalf of a people who had not yet repented as a body.

Gabriel arrives "about the time of the evening sacrifice," verse 21. In Babylon there was no temple and no altar, so this is the hour that Daniel keeps by memory and faith. Later Jews and Christians continued to pray at the hours of the sacrifices, Acts 3:1. The Persian decree that Gabriel mentions was historically unfolded in stages, in the edicts of Cyrus, Ezra 1:1 to 4, and later of Artaxerxes, Ezra 7:11 to 26, and the commission to Nehemiah, Nehemiah 2:1 to 8, and this is why interpreters disagree about where the sixty-nine weeks begin.
context.canonical:
Daniel 9 is a short anthology of the Old Testament. The prayer draws on Leviticus 26, where God warned that if His people refused discipline He would multiply their punishment "seven times," and where He promised that if they confessed their guilt and the guilt of their fathers He would remember His covenant, Leviticus 26:40 to 42. Daniel's prayer is that confession. It also draws on the pattern of Solomon at the dedication, 1 Kings 8:46 to 50, and it is matched in the days of the return by the prayers of Ezra, Ezra 9:6 to 15, and Nehemiah, Nehemiah 1:5 to 11 and 9:5 to 37. These leaders read the same disaster in the same way: a righteous God, a guilty people, and no appeal but mercy.

Gabriel's reply turns the "seventy years" into "seventy sevens." That reworking of a prophecy is already anticipated in Leviticus 26, where the penalty is repeated sevenfold, and in the Sabbath and jubilee cycles of Leviticus 25. The exile was a time of rest for the land; the seventy sevens will be the larger cycle in which God brings real rest from sin.

In the New Testament the chapter surfaces in several ways. Jesus warns of "the abomination of desolation, spoken of by the prophet Daniel," Matthew 24:15 and Mark 13:14, and Luke records that Jerusalem will be surrounded by armies, Luke 21:20. Luke's genealogy and his opening scenes are full of Gabriel, who appears to Zechariah at the hour of incense and to Mary, Luke 1:11 to 19 and 1:26. Hebrews draws out the language of sacrifice and atonement, especially Hebrews 9:11 to 14 and 9:24 to 26, where Christ appears once at the end of the ages to put away sin. The New Testament never quotes Daniel 9:24 to 27 in a complete chain, which is a reason for modesty about the exact scheme, but its main goals are plainly at work in the gospel.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The book of Daniel was written for people who lived under foreign rule and wondered if God had lost control. Daniel 9 meant to teach them two things at once. First, how to pray: with the Scriptures open, with the confession in the first person plural, and with the plea resting wholly on the character of God and not on the merit of the pray-er. Daniel was among the most faithful men in the book and yet he says "we have sinned," never "they."

Second, the chapter wanted to teach that the end of exile in Babylon was not the end of the story. Readers who expected the seventy years to settle everything were told that the return was a first step. The deeper trouble was sin, and the holy city and its people needed something that a Persian decree could not give. The numbers in verses 24 to 27 were not given to feed speculation about dates; they gave a long horizon of hope, with a sequence of rebuilding, an anointed one, destruction and a final reckoning, to people who would otherwise think in terms of a few decades. The chapter intends to humble the reader, to steady the reader, and to point the reader forward.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The prayer is a record of what one man did, but it is a model, and the text shows why. Daniel does not tell us to pray exactly these words. He shows a posture that Scripture elsewhere commands: confess sin, stand on God's promises, and ask for the sake of His name, Psalm 79:9 and 1 John 1:9. The fasting, sackcloth and ashes of verse 3 describe a custom of mourning for that time and place. The principle that behind them, a serious and humble seeking of God, carries forward; the particular outward form is not commanded.

The seventy sevens are different. They are a prophecy, not an instruction. They tell us what God has decreed, not what we are to do, and so the right response is not calculation but trust and watchfulness. The danger lies in treating them as a timetable by which to date events in our own day. Jesus said that no one knows the day or hour, Matthew 24:36, and Gabriel's own words in this chapter are about the story God had decreed for Daniel's people and holy city, not a calendar for later generations.

debates.question: How are the seventy weeks to be reckoned?

views.label: Seventy times seven years, running to Christ
views.case: Many early Christian writers and most Reformed readers take each week as seven years, giving 490 years. The sixty-nine weeks, 483 years, reach to the Anointed One, and the cutting off of verse 26 is the cross. On this view the decree of Artaxerxes in Ezra 7 or Nehemiah 2 is the starting point, and the six goals of verse 24 are accomplished by Christ's work. The strength is that the sequence leads to a cut off Anointed One who atones, which matches the gospel.

views.label: Seventy sevens with a gap before the last week
views.case: Dispensational readers agree about the sixty-nine weeks but place a long interval between the sixty-ninth and seventieth, with the last week still future, tied to a coming ruler who makes and breaks a covenant. They point to the fact that verse 26 puts the cutting off, and the destruction of the city, after the sixty-two weeks, not within the seventieth. Critics reply that the text gives no sign of a gap.

views.label: A symbolic or Maccabean reading
views.case: Some scholars take the numbers as symbolic, a long period of perfection that is not meant to be counted, and others read the chapter as pointing to the time of Antiochus IV, about 167 BC, with the anointed one as a high priest such as Onias III. The defiling of the temple in verse 27 certainly resembles what Antiochus did. Others answer that the full goals of verse 24, everlasting righteousness, cannot be exhausted by the second century BC.

debates.bearing: Faithful interpreters have held each of these views. What every one of them keeps is the central claim of verse 24, that God has set a decreed course to finish sin and bring in everlasting righteousness, and that the Anointed One's death is part of it. The text gives enough certainty to hope; it does not give enough to date the end.

debates.question: Who is the "he" who confirms a covenant with many in verse 27?

views.label: The Anointed One
views.case: The nearest masculine subject in the sentence is the Anointed One of verse 26. On this view, the one who confirms a covenant with many is Christ, who said His blood was poured out for many, Mark 14:24, and the ending of sacrifice in the middle of the week is the effect of His death, since a final offering makes the others obsolete, Hebrews 10:11 to 14.

views.label: The prince who is to come
views.case: Others note that the closest grammatical antecedent is actually the prince of verse 26, whose people destroy the city. On this view a hostile ruler, whether Titus's Rome or a coming antichrist, makes a treaty and then breaks it, and sets up the abomination. This fits Jesus' use of the abomination of desolation as an ominous warning, Matthew 24:15.

debates.bearing: The grammar alone does not settle it, so the reader weighs it against the whole book and the New Testament. Whichever is chosen, the chapter's pattern is the same: the Anointed One's work is the hope, and the desolating prince's work is the warning.

study.originalLanguages:
Start with the verb Daniel uses for what he did with Jeremiah. He "understood," bin, "from the books," a plural word that suggests a collection of scrolls. The same verb is what Gabriel asks of him in verses 22 and 23, where the angel comes to give "understanding" and tells him to "understand the vision." Daniel's reading leads to understanding, and understanding leads to prayer, and prayer leads to a fuller understanding. It is a small picture of how Scripture is meant to be read.

The covenant name of God, the LORD, in Hebrew the four letters of the name revealed at the burning bush, is used in Daniel only in this chapter, verses 2, 4, 8, 10, 13, 14 and 20. Elsewhere he speaks of "God," "God of heaven," or "the Most High." Here, where he pleads on the basis of a covenant that Israel broke, he uses the covenant name. That detail reveals what the prayer rests on: not the generic fact that there is a God, but the personal promise-keeping Lord of Exodus 3 and 34.

The four verbs of confession in verse 5, "sinned," "done wrong," "acted wickedly," and "rebelled," build from missing the mark to twisting the path to guilty wrongdoing to open revolt. The first three appear together in Solomon's prayer, 1 Kings 8:47, which hoped that exiles who confessed in this manner would be heard. The first three are about conduct, and the fourth, marad, is political: it is the word of a vassal who throws off a king. Daniel names the whole range.

Verse 7 sets two nouns against each other: tsedaqah, "righteousness," belongs to God, and boshet panim, "shame of face," belongs to the people. In verse 16 the plural tsidqot refers to God's "righteous acts," the saving deeds by which He has put things right in the past, and verse 18 says that Israel does not rest on its own tsidqot but on God's rachamim, "compassion," a word related to the womb. Righteousness here is not only a standard but a power to deliver. That is why Daniel can ask God, in the name of His righteousness, to turn away anger.

Gabriel's message turns on the number seventy and on the word translated "decreed," nechtak, which literally means "cut off" or "determined." The six goals in verse 24 are expressed with infinitives and they pair up: three about sin, "to finish transgression, to seal up sin, to atone for iniquity," and three about restoration, "to bring in everlasting righteousness, to seal vision and prophecy, to anoint a most holy." The BSB footnote notes the last may be "the Most Holy One," so it can refer to a person or a place.

The word mashiach in verses 25 and 26 has no article in Hebrew. It was used for priests, Leviticus 4:3, for kings, 1 Samuel 24:6, and even for Cyrus, Isaiah 45:1. It is not yet the fixed title it later became, and in verse 25 it is paired with nagid, "prince" or "leader." The verb "cut off," yikkaret, is the verb used in the Torah for being cut off from the people, Genesis 17:14, and also for cutting a covenant. Both senses lie near the surface of a text that is about a cut off person and a covenant confirmed with many.

Finally, the verb "poured out" in verse 27, tittak, is the same verb as in verse 11, where Daniel confessed that the curse of the Law "has been poured out" on Israel. The last line of the chapter says the decreed destruction is "poured out" on the desolator. The curse that fell on Israel returns to fall on the one who desolates, a verbal link that ties the prayer to the prophecy.

typology.fulfillment: Daniel is blameless in the book, yet he prays "we have sinned." He stands with a guilty people, takes their guilt on his lips, and pleads for their forgiveness on grounds outside them. That is the shape of priestly mediation, as in Moses at Exodus 32:11 to 14 and Ezra at Ezra 9:6. It reaches its fullness in Christ, who is without sin and yet is made sin on our behalf, 2 Corinthians 5:21, and who lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25. The type falls short because Daniel includes himself among the guilty and can only ask. Christ gives what is asked.

typology.type: The seventy years and the sevens of Sabbath rest, Daniel 9:2 and 24
typology.fulfillment: The exile was counted as Sabbaths owed to the land, Leviticus 26:34 and 2 Chronicles 36:21, and Gabriel multiplies the pattern into seventy sevens, the shape of the jubilee, which freed slaves and returned land, Leviticus 25:8 to 10. In Nazareth, Jesus read Isaiah's words about the year of the Lord's favor and said they were fulfilled in the hearing of His hearers, Luke 4:18 to 21. The rest that Israel's calendar kept promising is found in Him, Matthew 11:28. The type falls short because the jubilee released debts and land for a season, while His release deals with sin for good, Hebrews 4:9 to 10.

typology.type: The evening sacrifice and the time of the answer, Daniel 9:21
typology.fulfillment: The answer comes as the hour of the evening sacrifice, which Daniel can no longer offer in a ruined temple. The daily offering was the standing request of Israel to be accepted, Exodus 29:38 to 42. The Gospels say that Jesus died in the afternoon, at the ninth hour, Matthew 27:45 to 50, the hour of the afternoon offering and of prayer in the temple, Acts 3:1. The text does not say this is a deliberate design, so it should be held lightly. What can be said is that the sacrificial system was never meant to be self-sufficient, and Hebrews 10:11 to 14 shows that its repeated offerings give way to one.

typology.type: The desolate sanctuary and the place made most holy, Daniel 9:17 and 24
typology.fulfillment: Daniel asks that God's face shine on a sanctuary that is desolate, and the answer says that a most holy will be anointed. The tabernacle and temple were anointed with oil, Exodus 40:9, and Jesus speaks of the temple of His body being raised, John 2:19 to 21. Hebrews says He entered not a hand made sanctuary but heaven itself, Hebrews 9:11 and 9:24. The New Testament also calls believers the temple of the living God, 2 Corinthians 6:16, and describes the final city as having no temple because God is its temple, Revelation 21:22. The type falls short because every earthly sanctuary could be profaned, as verse 27 shows, but the new one cannot.

study.christ:
Gabriel's six goals in verse 24 are best read as a description of what the Anointed One does, and the New Testament speaks of each of them in terms of Jesus. To finish transgression and put an end to sin is what John the Baptist points to when he says, "Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world," John 1:29. To atone for iniquity is the language of Romans 3:25, where God presents Christ as the propitiation, and of Hebrews 2:17. To bring in everlasting righteousness is the burden of Romans 3:21 to 26 and 2 Corinthians 5:21: a righteousness from God that does not run out. To seal up vision and prophecy is to bring it to its goal; Jesus told the disciples that everything written about Him in the Law, the Prophets and the Psalms had to be fulfilled, Luke 24:44. And to anoint a most holy, whether a place or a person, fits the one who is called the Christ, the Anointed, Acts 10:38, and who opens the way into the Holy of Holies, Hebrews 10:19 to 20.

The verb in verse 26, that the Anointed One is "cut off and will have nothing," is the closest that the Old Testament comes in this chapter to the suffering of Isaiah 53:8, where the Servant is cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of the people. The one who is cut off here is not cut off for his own sins, which is why the next clause is a quiet shock: it is the people of the coming prince who will destroy the city, as if the cutting off of the Anointed One and the ruin of Jerusalem belong in a single sentence, which is how Jesus Himself spoke when He wept over the city, Luke 19:41 to 44.

The covenant language is worth pausing on. Verse 27 speaks of a covenant confirmed with "many." At the Last Supper Jesus takes the cup and calls it His blood of the covenant poured out for many, Mark 14:24. Whether verse 27 refers to Him directly or not, the word "many" becomes part of how the New Testament speaks of the scope of His work, Isaiah 53:11 to 12 and Romans 5:15.

The best guard against forced allegory is that the chapter must stand on its own terms. Daniel asks about a city and sanctuary, and the answer concerns that same city and sanctuary. The text does not name Jesus, and its numbers are disputed. Yet the center of it, that sin must be atoned for by an Anointed One who is cut off, and that this precedes everlasting righteousness, is exactly the pattern of the gospel. Daniel prayed that God would act for His own sake, verse 19, and in the cross God did, showing Himself both righteous and the one who justifies, Romans 3:26.
study.god:
The prayer insists on holding together what we are tempted to separate. God is "great and awesome," verse 4, and yet He "keeps covenant." He is righteous in everything He does, verse 14, and yet compassion and forgiveness belong to Him, verse 9. Daniel never asks God to shrink the justice of the exile in order to make the request sound better; he agrees with the verdict, and then pleads for mercy within it. This is the doctrine of God that makes repentance possible: a Judge who is not arbitrary and a Father who is not indifferent.

The prayer also shows the God who has been faithful to His own word even in judgment. The disaster of verse 12 came because God "carried out the words" He had spoken against His people. Those words were in the Law, Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The same reliability that grounds the curse grounds the hope, because the same Law promises restoration to those who confess, Leviticus 26:40 to 45. That God keeps His threats is the best reason to trust His promises.

God is shown acting "for Your own sake," verses 17 and 19. That is not self-centeredness in the human sense. The city and people "bear Your name," verse 19, so God's reputation in the world is tied to their rescue, as it was at the Exodus, verse 15. Ezekiel gives the same logic, Ezekiel 36:22 to 32. It is good news for the guilty, because their hope is anchored in God's character rather than their performance.

Finally, God speaks and moves quickly. An answer "went out" at the start of the petitions, verse 23, and Gabriel is sent in flight before Daniel finishes. He answers beyond the question: Daniel asked about a city and received a plan stretching across centuries. God is not only responsive but patient in His design, giving a timetable in which sin is reckoned with and not merely suspended. For worship, the chapter teaches that the way to approach this God is with the Scriptures in hand, our own sin on our lips, and His name as our argument.

crossReferences.note: The text Daniel is reading. Babylon will serve for seventy years, and then God will punish Babylon itself. Daniel notices that the clock set by the prophet is nearly run and takes the promise as a reason to pray, not a reason to relax.

The promised path of repentance for an exiled people: they confess their iniquity and that of their fathers, the uncircumcised heart is humbled, and God remembers His covenant. Daniel's prayer is this confession carried out, down to the double reference to fathers, verse 16.

At the temple's dedication Solomon foresaw exile and asked God to hear those who say they have sinned and acted wickedly and turned back, so Daniel prays toward a temple that is in ruins in the very words Solomon supplied.

Nehemiah prays in the same pattern, calling God great and awesome and keeping covenant, then confessing the sins of his father's house and himself, and then appealing to God's promise to regather. It shows that Daniel's prayer became a model for the returning community.

God says that He will restore Israel not for their sake but for the sake of His holy name, which they profaned among the nations, and will give a new heart. It supports the logic of Daniel 9:17 to 19, where the plea rests on God's name, not Israel's worth.

The Servant is cut off from the land of the living for the transgression of the people. The cutting off of the Anointed One in Daniel 9:26 reads naturally alongside it: both speak of a death that is judicial and yet is not the death of a sinner.

Gabriel, who explained the vision to Daniel, is sent to Mary with news of a son who will be given the throne of David. The same messenger who announced the Anointed One's coming in Daniel tells of His arrival in Nazareth.

Jesus tells His disciples that when they see the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel standing in the holy place, they are to flee. He treats the prophecy as still having a further fulfilment ahead and uses it to warn, not to puzzle.

Christ enters the greater and more perfect tent not with the blood of goats and calves but with His own blood, securing eternal redemption and cleansing the conscience. This is the final form of the atonement for iniquity promised in Daniel 9:24.

Priests stand daily offering sacrifices that can never take away sins, but Christ offered one sacrifice and sat down. This clarifies how sacrifice and offering can be brought to an end, as Daniel 9:27 says, by the offering that makes the others unnecessary.

God's righteousness is revealed apart from the Law, and He put forward Christ as a propitiation, that He might be just and the justifier. It answers Daniel's contrast of divine righteousness and human shame, and shows how everlasting righteousness is brought in.

Ezra rises from fasting at the evening sacrifice to pray in torn garments, confessing guilt that has reached the heavens, and thanks God for a little reviving in bondage. It matches Daniel's posture and shows that mourning for sin was a mark of the faithful remnant.

study.oneStory:
The story of the Bible is a cycle of breaking and mending, and Daniel 9 sits at the lowest point of the breaking. The garden had been lost in Genesis 3, the land was promised to Abraham, the kingdom was established under David, and now the land is empty, the city in rubble, and the temple gone. Moses had warned that this could happen and had also promised, in the same chapter of Leviticus, that a confessing people would be remembered. Daniel prays in the gap between those two sentences of Moses.

His prayer shows what the faithful do in the dark: they read, they agree with God about their guilt, and they hold God to His own character. It is a pattern that runs from Abraham pleading for Sodom, Genesis 18:23 to 33, to Moses at Sinai, Exodus 32:11 to 14, to the confessions of Ezra and Nehemiah, and on to the cry of the tax collector in the temple, Luke 18:13.

Gabriel's answer sets the course for everything that follows in the biblical story. Return from exile will happen, but the plot will not end with it. Another decree, another stage of rebuilding, an Anointed One and a destruction will follow. The Old Testament closes with a rebuilt but modest temple and a people still waiting, Malachi 3:1. The New Testament begins with a man of the exile's long hope, Simeon, waiting for the consolation of Israel, Luke 2:25, and with Gabriel again sent to announce that the waiting has changed.

The cross is where the prayer is finally answered. The desolation Daniel wept over, the broken covenant, the curse poured out, all of it falls on the Anointed One who is cut off, Galatians 3:13, so that the blessing might come to all nations. The Bible then ends where Daniel's prayer wanted to go: a city that bears God's name, where nothing accursed remains and no temple is needed, Revelation 21:2 and 22:3 to 4. The same city whose desolation Daniel mourned is, in its final form, a city whose lamp is the Lamb.

quiz.q: What prompted Daniel's prayer of confession?

options.text: Reading in Jeremiah that the seventy years of Jerusalem's desolation were nearly complete.
options.note: Daniel 9:2 shows him moved to pray by the Scriptures.

options.text: A frightening new dream he could not interpret.
options.note: This prayer was prompted by reading Jeremiah, not by a dream.

options.text: A command from King Darius to fast.
options.note: Daniel turned to prayer on his own, moved by Scripture.

options.text: A festival that required public confession.
options.note: It was his reading of Jeremiah's prophecy that led him to pray.

quiz.q: On what basis did Daniel ask God to forgive?

options.text: Not on Israel's righteousness, but on God's great compassion and for the sake of His own name.
options.note: Daniel 9:18-19 rests the plea entirely on God's mercy and name.

options.text: On the many good deeds of the exiles.
options.note: Daniel explicitly denies any appeal to their righteous acts.

options.text: On a bargain to rebuild the temple quickly.
options.note: He offered no bargain, only appeal to God's mercy.

options.text: On his own personal holiness.
options.note: He confessed sin and pleaded God's compassion, not his own merit.

quiz.q: What are the goals of the seventy weeks in verse 24?

options.text: To finish transgression, end sin, make atonement, and bring in everlasting righteousness.
options.note: Daniel 9:24 lists the sixfold saving purpose fulfilled in Christ.

options.text: Only to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem.
options.note: Rebuilding is mentioned, but the deep goal is dealing with sin forever.

options.text: To crown a new earthly king in Babylon.
options.note: The goal is atonement and righteousness, not a Babylonian coronation.

options.text: To end all prophecy and Scripture.
options.note: It seals up vision, but the heart is atonement and everlasting righteousness.

quiz.q: What does the prophecy say happens to the Messiah, the Prince?

options.text: After the appointed weeks He is cut off and has nothing, that is, He dies.
options.note: Daniel 9:26 foretells the Anointed One being cut off.

options.text: He conquers Rome and reigns from Jerusalem at once.
options.note: The prophecy foretells His being cut off, not an immediate earthly reign.

options.text: He remains hidden and never appears.
options.note: He comes and is cut off; He does appear.

options.text: He becomes king of Babylon.
options.note: He is the Anointed One who is cut off, not a Babylonian king.

quiz.q: How is the seventy weeks prophecy fulfilled in Jesus?

options.text: As the Anointed One cut off, He makes atonement for iniquity and brings in everlasting righteousness at the cross.
options.note: The sixfold goal is accomplished in Christ's death, Hebrews 9:26.

options.text: It has no fulfillment in Jesus, only in ancient politics.
options.note: The saving goals of verse 24 are fulfilled in Christ, whatever the chronology debates.

options.text: It teaches Jesus would avoid death entirely.
options.note: The opposite; the Messiah is cut off, pointing to His atoning death.

options.text: It predicts Jesus would rebuild Babylon.
options.note: It foretells atonement through the Anointed One, fulfilled at the cross.

questions: Daniel confessed not only his people's sins but joined himself to them, saying we have sinned. How does honest, humble confession shape your own prayers?
Daniel appealed to God's mercy and name, not to any goodness of his own. Where are you tempted to approach God on the basis of your record rather than His grace?
Reading Scripture moved Daniel to pray. How might letting God's word set the agenda change the way you pray?
Gabriel said the answer went out at the very beginning of Daniel's prayer. How does it encourage you to know God hears the moment you begin to pray?
The seventy weeks pointed to the Messiah who makes atonement for sin. How does resting in Christ's finished atonement free you from trying to cover your own guilt?

translationNotes.note: Loving devotion renders chesed, God's steadfast covenant love, the ground on which Daniel's whole prayer rests.
Seventy weeks may be rendered seventy sevens; the Most Holy Place may also be rendered the Most Holy One, leaving room for a personal, messianic sense.
Messiah, the Prince may be rendered the Anointed One; the title carries both royal and priestly overtones, fulfilled in Christ.
The abomination that causes desolation is a phrase Jesus takes up in Matthew 24:15; the exact chronology of the final week is much debated and held with humility.
